rationale: bugs_open/191. RenderSiteComponentsAction builds a site's header nav items and its header CTA button in ONE run, from ONE pages table, and validates them with TWO DIFFERENT eligibility predicates. Nav items go through loadFetchablePageSet (nav_tables.go:258): status NOT IN ('deleted','archived') AND NOT(datahelpers.NeverDeployedPagePredicate). The header CTA went through loadResolverPageSet (resolve_internal_links_action.go:486): the status floor only, with NO deployment check at all. So a page that has never deployed passes the CTA check and its URL is written into site_components.header. Confirmed live at the wire on 2026-08-04: mortgagecalculator.co.uk ships a header whose nav had been filtered down to its single deployed page, and whose CTA button beside it points at /tools/stamp-duty/index.html (build_status='planned', deployed_at IS NULL) which curls HTTP 404. Chrome renders on EVERY page, so this is one 404 button per page, and the chrome render is idempotence-gated so nothing re-renders it when the target finally deploys. The structural half, and the reason a smaller patch would not hold: the two escapes that make the nav's filter safe (lookup error, and zero deployed pages on a first build) were written INLINE inside applyNavVisibility, so no other caller could reuse the policy they encode even if its author had known to. That is why the CTA reached for the nearest other helper. This is the direct sibling of bugs_closed/118 (commit b052249d8), which fixed 'which library component serves chrome function F?' answered three ways with one named predicate, one resolver and a source-scanning lockstep test; 118 fixed component eligibility and explicitly did not touch link-target eligibility. This change applies that same construction to link targets. Intent: make 'which page may a piece of CHROME link to?' one named, tested decision that a future caller cannot get wrong by accident.
submitter: bugfix_191_chrome_link_policy (session picking up unowned bugs from bugs_open)

plan.summary: Extract the chrome link-target decision (the fetchable page set plus its two escapes) out of applyNavVisibility into a named ChromeLinkPolicy type, and route BOTH chrome consumers through it: the nav filter, and the header CTA fallback that previously used the loose page-content set. No new spelling of the deployment predicate is introduced — the policy calls the existing loadFetchablePageSet, whose SQL is untouched and still builds from datahelpers.NeverDeployedPagePredicate. The page-CONTENT callers of loadResolverPageSet are deliberately unchanged and the boundary is documented on the function itself, with a source-scanning allow-list test so a fourth caller cannot quietly hand-roll a loose set for a chrome link.

edits.rationale: The one named decision. It calls the existing loadFetchablePageSet (so the deployment predicate keeps exactly one definition) and holds the two escapes that were previously inline in applyNavVisibility and therefore unreachable from the CTA path. Allows() also carries the ClassifyLinkScope guard, so external/mailto/anchor hrefs are never judged against the pages table.
THE FIX. The CTA now consults the same policy as the nav rendered beside it, in both places it tested a URL: the contact-derived ctaURL and the chooseCTATargets fallback pick.

Eliminate the inline copy of the escape logic, or the policy exists in two places and the 191 class survives its own fix. Behaviour is deliberately unchanged: the proof is that nav_visibility_test.go (10 subtests) passes UNEDITED. The SET-level rescue (len(kept)==0) deliberately stays here rather than moving into the policy: it is a property of a menu, not of a URL, and it does not transfer to a lone button — an absent CTA is a legitimate render, an absent menu is not.

Comment only, no code change. The boundary has to be written where the next reader is standing, because the two helpers are one word apart and picking the wrong one is invisible in review. States why the looseness is correct for page content and forbidden for chrome, and names the test that enforces the caller allow-list.
edits.sketch:
+// loadResolverPageSet is the PAGE-CONTENT link-target set: every page the
+// platform intends to serve, status floor only, with NO deployment predicate.
+// That looseness is deliberate — a batch build resolves page A's CTA before
+// page B deploys minutes later, and a content CTA is re-resolved on every page
+// render and rerender, so a not-yet-shipped target is corrected by the next
+// pass rather than frozen.
+//
+// CHROME MAY NOT USE THIS SET (bugs_open/191). Chrome ships on every page,
+// renders once behind an idempotence gate, and has no repair pass, so the same
+// looseness there is a site-wide 404 nothing later fixes. Chrome link targets
+// go through LoadChromeLinkPolicy (chrome_link_policy.go). The caller
+// allow-list for this function is enforced by chrome_link_policy_test.go.
 func loadResolverPageSet(...)

edits.rationale: Four behavioural tests plus the door. The scans skip comment lines (so the doc comments above and every historical comment naming loadResolverPageSet stay legal), each has a gone-blind Fatal, an allow-listed file that produces ZERO matches is a Fatal (an allow-list that matches nothing is a scan that has stopped seeing), and a synthetic-line test proves the matcher still fires. ALL FOUR GUARDS ARE MUTATION-PROVEN, in a git-archive-HEAD copy: revert the CTA call site -> both scans RED; drop the deployment predicate from the fetchable SQL -> 5 RED; disable the zero-deployed escape (condition flipped to ==-1 so the mutant still compiles) -> 2 RED; make Allows permanently true -> 2 RED.

Registered in the SAME commit that ships the seam, per the CLAUDE.md platform-seams ruling (condition 2, which is now the whole requirement). Carries both landmines: Allows() returns true for EVERYTHING when unfiltered so it is never a deployment proof; and the escape keys on the row COUNT, never on set emptiness, because loadFetchablePageSet always injects the site root. Also records the measured escape population and the open review question about whether the content path should ever converge.

plan.risks: 1) The refactor of applyNavVisibility is the main behavioural risk: it is meant to be a pure extraction. The control is that nav_visibility_test.go passes with ZERO edits — if it had needed an edit, the refactor changed behaviour and would be wrong. Reviewers should check the Warn count per escape is still exactly 1 (the tests assert log counts) and that group_types still rides on the escape Warns, now via logger.With. 2) ONE behaviour is changed deliberately and reviewers should judge it: on a lookup ERROR the CTA previously rendered no button (a side effect of loadResolverPageSet returning an empty set on error, not a considered policy) and now goes unfiltered like the nav. The argument is that chrome is idempotence-gated, so a button dropped during one failed render may never get a second chance, and answering the freeze one way for the nav and the other way for the button beside it would reproduce this bug's own shape inside its fix. The counter-argument, which bugs_open/191 itself proposed, is that no button is the safer outcome; if the council prefers that, the change is one branch in LoadChromeLinkPolicy's caller, not a redesign. 3) The strict arm can now REMOVE a CTA button that renders today on a site with unbuilt targets — that is the intended fix (the button was a 404), but it means a header can go from having a button to having none on the next chrome render. The gated template already handles an empty cta_url by rendering no button, so this is a supported state, not a broken one. 4) Scope: the two page-CONTENT callers of loadResolverPageSet are deliberately untouched; tightening them would strip CTAs from most of every fresh build and would redefine the unresolved_cta HITL signal (LNK-012), which is a separate fleet-wide change. Reviewers who think the content path should also tighten should say so as a follow-up rather than widening this one. 5) The source-scanning tests make the ALLOW-LIST load-bearing: renaming resolve_internal_links_action.go or rerender_page_sections_action.go without updating loosePageSetAllowed turns the scan into a Fatal — deliberately, because an allow-list entry matching nothing means the scan has stopped seeing.
